title: DAX UDF Parameter Modes: Stop Using VAL and EXPR Wrong

entities.name: DAX
entities.quote: You saw DAX user defined functions and thought nice, reusable code.

quotes.text: In DAX UDFs, the parameter passing mode is not decoration. It's semantics. It changes when evaluation happens, which changes what result you get.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: States why choosing between VAL and EXPR changes the meaning of a function.

quotes.text: Passing an expression does not automatically give you context transition. The measures get an implicit calculate when used inside a row context, row expressions do not.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains the subtle trap behind UDFs that ignore the current row.

quotes.text: Instead of spraying calculate metric XPR across your iterators like confetti, you compute the metric exactly once per entity, customer product date, and attach it as a temporary column to a small table.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Describes the materialization pattern that removes repeated evaluation cost.

quotes.text: Types are not your safety net, they are your contract. Use them to communicate intent, not to correct sloppy callers.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A clear principle for declaring parameter types in UDFs.

quotes.text: Designed for the caller you have distracted, hurried, occasionally wrong, and put the correctness inside the function. That's how you build UDFs that won't betray you later.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Summarizes the design philosophy for robust, self-sufficient DAX functions.

chapters.title: Why VAL vs EXPR matters in DAX UDFs
The two parameter modes: VAL and EXPR

takeaways: Use VAL for fixed scalars evaluated once in the caller's context and EXPR for formulas that must re-evaluate under the filters and iterators inside the function.
An EXPR parameter does not get context transition automatically, so wrap every evaluation of it in CALCULATE inside the UDF instead of relying on callers.
When an EXPR is used more than once, materialize it once per entity with ADDCOLUMNS and reuse the column, and choose parameter types that match the math to avoid silent truncation.
hook: DAX user-defined functions can return numbers that look right but are silently wrong when VAL and EXPR parameter modes are mixed up. This episode is for Power BI and Fabric modelers writing reusable DAX. It explains parameter modes, context transition, materialization with ADDCOLUMNS and type casting, with a checklist for UDFs you can trust.
